children: By Mark R. Long

The average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. broke above $6 for the first time Friday, the WSJ's Shradha Dinesh reports. The price of the fuel has risen 14% in the past month and more than 60% in the past year, as American exports surge to fill a gap in global supplies crimped by the closure of the Strait of Hormmuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.

Gasoline prices also continue to forge higher. The average price of a gallon was $4.295, AAA said, up more than 40% since the Iran war started. U.S. gas prices rose 3.9% in August from July, accounting for more than a third of the monthly increase in the prices of all items, according to the Labor Department.

Nevertheless, beyond the fuel pump and airline terminal, there are few signs yet that these soaring fuel costs are filtering into the broader economy, the Journal's Konrad Putzier writes. This raises the question of whether and when they will start boosting prices for other goods and services.
Saudi Arabia shut down the crucial East-West pipeline that allowed the kingdom to export oil after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, saying it had been attacked by drones fired from Iraq. (WSJ)
Oil output from Saudi Arabia plummeted to 6.24 million barrels a day in August, the lowest in more than three decades, because of Houthi attacks, the International Energy Agency said. (WSJ)
A recovery in Mideast oil flows is expected to stretch into next year as attacks on Gulf shipping and Houthi threats in the Red Sea strain key energy arteries, the IEA said. (WSJ)
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth says the global oil inventories and other market buffers that helped cap crude prices for months have "largely now played out." (WSJ)
Spot rates for very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, have risen to their highest levels ever. (Lloyd's List)
"Diesel prices right now are a major concern for us."  White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett
Manufacturing & Trade

Stellantis is in talks to sell its idled Toronto-area factory to Roshel, a local maker of armored vehicles, the WSJ's Paul Vieira reports. The discussions prompted the union representing over 9,000 of the automaker's Canadian employees to declare an impasse on talks toward a new labor deal.
The potential sale is the latest development involving the (Stellantis) factory in Brampton, Ontario, which hasn't operated since 2024 to undergo retooling.

Stellantis last year unveiled plans to shift the production of its next-generation Jeep Compass to Illinois from Brampton after the Trump administration slapped steep tariffs on foreign-made cars. The decision sparked the threat of a lawsuit from the Canadian government, which had provided Stellantis with hundreds of millions of dollars for work at the plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ontario.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is accelerating a strategic pivot to Europe following the collapse of trade talks with the U.S., and will host an investment summit in Toronto to attract global capital. (WSJ)
Sen. Susan Collins (R., Maine) is working with Trump administration officials to lessen the impact of the escalating U.S. trade dispute with Canada. (WSJ)
President Trump said he plans to rescind the U.S.'s 10% tariff on Irish whiskey. (WSJ)
Number of the Day
Combined loaded container imports into the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach in August, in 20-foot equivalent units, down 1.1% from July but up 1.22% from a year earlier.
In Other News
The U.S. inflation rate held steady at 3.4% in August, even with July's 3.4%, the Labor Department said, though a key measure of underlying price trends came in stronger than expected. (WSJ)

Lettuce prices are still wilting after the cyclosporiasis outbreak, with the index for lettuce inflation falling a seasonally adjusted 6.2% in August from July, according to the Labor Department. (WSJ)
The University of Michigan's preliminary consumer sentiment index fell to 47.8 in September from 51.7 at the end of August. (WSJ)
U.K. economic growth rose unexpectedly in July following a strong start to the year, despite a rise in energy prices due to the Iran war. (WSJ)
Amazon is pausing its operations with 21 Air, the cargo carrier that operated an Amazon-branded plane that crashed in Miami, killing five people. (WSJ)
Kroger lowered its full-year same-store sales outlook, as shoppers' budget constraints and concerns about cyclospora resulted in lower spending. (WSJ)
French drugmaker Ipsen is considering building a production site in the U.S. (WSJ)
The EPA removed online resources for companies about measuring the carbon footprint of their supply chains, known as Scope 3 emissions. (Bloomberg)
New York City redesigned its truck-route system for the first time since the 1970s, aiming to shift more trucks away from residential streets. (SupplyChain24/7)
Warehouse-robot maker Vecna Robotics has raised $31 million in venture-capital backing, aiming to boost commercial sales and to accelerate development of new capabilities. (DC Velocity)
FedEx launched a tool to allow merchants to show a duty and tax guarantee to customers at checkout, to head off surprise import costs charged later on. (SupplyChainDive)
